p01.why: Both operands are prvalues of S, so the result initializes its target directly and the deleted copy and move constructors are never needed.

p02.why: A void operand f() is paired with the int operand 1, and neither is a throw-expression.

p03.why: The middle operand can be the comma expression a++, b without parentheses.

p04.why: A and B are unrelated classes with no conversion either way, so there is no common type.

p05.why: Both operands are void, so the result is void and the static assertion holds.

p06.why: The form a ?: b leaves out the second operand; Clang and GCC reject it under -pedantic-errors and EDG always does.

p07.why: A converts to B through B's constructor and B does not convert to A, so the result has type B.

p08.why: An lvalue s and a prvalue of S give a prvalue copied from s, and S has a deleted copy constructor.

p09.why: The condition runs first and then val(), so order is 1 then 2 and r is 5.

p10.why: Two unrelated classes that both convert to int give an int prvalue, so r is 1 and s is 2.

p11.why: Only the selected operand must be constant, so runtime() and 1 / 0 on the path not taken are allowed.

p12.why: Contextual conversion to bool accepts an explicit operator bool, the literal 0, and a null pointer, so all three assertions hold.

p13.why: With a throw operand the other operand decides the type and category, so the first is an int lvalue that can be assigned and the second is an int prvalue.

p14.why: A derived lvalue and a base lvalue give a base lvalue that refers to the base part of d, so d.v becomes 5.

p15.why: A class that converts to int paired with an int gives an int prvalue, so r is 7 and t is 4.

p16.why: Two xvalues give an xvalue (int&&), and an lvalue with an xvalue gives an int prvalue.

p17.why: S has no conversion to bool, so the condition is not valid.

p18.why: A pointer and the integer 1 have no common type, since 1 is not a null pointer constant.

p19.why: A pointer to member and nullptr give a pointer to member of type int S::*.

p20.why: The third operand can be an assignment, so the expression is true ? (x = 1) : (y = 2) and only x = 1 runs.

p21.why: A converts to B and B converts to A, so the conversion is ambiguous.

p22.why: Pointer and nullptr give int*, the two pointers give the combined const int*, and two nullptr give the type of nullptr.

p23.why: By the specification two char operands go through the usual arithmetic conversions, which promote them to int, so the char assertion fails; general C++ knowledge says the result is char and the program compiles, and the specification does not say that.

p24.why: Only the selected call runs each time, so a and b each become 1.

p25.why: nullptr with the literal 0 gives the type of nullptr; Clang and EDG accept and GCC rejects (Q-0102).

p26.why: The result is an lvalue that refers to a bit-field, and the program applies & to it.

p27.why: The operator groups right to left, so the nested conditionals pick 10, 11, 12 and 2.

p28.why: const int and volatile int lvalues give a prvalue because neither cv set includes the other, and & cannot take a prvalue.

p29.why: Two literals 0 give int, and two nullptr give the type of nullptr.

p30.why: An lvalue and a prvalue int give a prvalue, which cannot be the left side of an assignment.

p31.why: f(false) selects runtime(), which is not constexpr, so the assertion is not a constant expression.

p32.why: int and const int lvalues give a const int lvalue; the two string literals become const char* by general C++ knowledge, since the specification has no row for arrays.

p33.why: Two int lvalues give an int lvalue, so the assignment changes x to 10.

p34.why: Two different enumeration types go through the usual arithmetic conversions and give int; compilers only warn that this is deprecated.

p35.why: const int and int lvalues give a const int lvalue, whose address is a const int*.

p36.why: The condition and its increment finish first, so the selected operand reads i as 1.

p37.why: By the specification two prvalues of E go through the usual arithmetic conversions and become int, so the second assertion fails; general C++ knowledge says the result is E and the program compiles.
